MASTER PROMPT — EXACT SPEECH-TO-VISUAL ANIMATION SYNCHRONIZATION
Apply this prompt ONLY to the animation and visual timing system of the
existing video project.
The goal is:
EVERY VISUAL ACTION MUST HAPPEN AT THE EXACT MOMENT THE NARRATOR TALKS
ABOUT THAT ACTION.
Do NOT animate visuals independently of the narration.
Do NOT use generic scene-level fade-ins where the entire scene appears at
once.
Do NOT reveal a complete diagram before the narrator explains it.
Do NOT animate an object before its corresponding concept is spoken.
============================================================
CORE RULE
============================================================
VOICEOVER = MASTER TIMELINE.
The narration controls the timing of:
- visual appearances
- text appearances
- keyword highlights
- character gestures
- character reactions
- diagram construction
- node activation
- connector drawing
- arrows
- data movement
- chart animation
- counters
- progress bars
- UI interactions
- terminal typing
- image reveals
- object movement
- camera movement
- emphasis
- transitions.
Every meaningful animation must be synchronized to the exact speech segment
that explains it.
============================================================
SEMANTIC SPEECH SYNC
============================================================
Do NOT synchronize only by sentence.
Synchronize by MEANINGFUL PHRASE.
Example narration:
"The agent enters the sandbox and can access the workspace."
Do NOT animate the entire scene when the sentence starts.
Instead:
"When the agent enters"
→ animate the character entering the sandbox.
"the sandbox"
→ reveal/highlight the sandbox boundary.
"can access"
→ animate the permission/access indicator.
"the workspace"
→ reveal/highlight the workspace.
Each visual event must correspond to the exact phrase that describes it.
============================================================
WORD / PHRASE TIMELINE
============================================================
Create a semantic timing map:
{
  "speech": "the agent enters the sandbox",
  "start": 12.42,
  "end": 13.81,
  "visual": "agent enters sandbox",
  "animationStart": 12.42,
  "animationEnd": 13.20
}
Use actual audio timing whenever available.
If word-level timestamps are available, use them.
If only sentence timestamps are available, estimate phrase timing from the
audio and preserve the natural speech rhythm.
============================================================
EXACT EVENT RULE
============================================================
For every important phrase:
SPEECH START
↓
VISUAL EVENT START
The animation should begin when the relevant concept is spoken.
Example:
Narrator:
"the network is blocked"
At the word/phrase:
"network"
→ network becomes visible.
At:
"blocked"
→ network connection stops and blocked state activates.
Do not show "blocked" before the narrator says it.
============================================================
PROGRESSIVE VISUAL REVEAL
============================================================
Never show the final complex visual before it has been explained.
Build the visual as the narration builds the explanation.
Example:
Narrator:
"First, we have the host."
→ Host appears.
Narrator:
"Inside it is the sandbox."
→ Sandbox appears.
Narrator:
"The agent runs inside the sandbox."
→ Agent enters.
Narrator:
"Network access is restricted."
→ Network lines appear and become blocked.
The visual story must follow the spoken story.
============================================================
TEXT SYNCHRONIZATION
============================================================
Text must appear exactly when its concept is spoken.
Do NOT display:
"Sandbox"
before the narrator discusses the sandbox.
When the narrator says:
"sandbox"
→ reveal/highlight "SANDBOX".
When the narrator says:
"host"
→ reveal/highlight "HOST".
When the narrator emphasizes a keyword:
→ animate that keyword.
Use:
scale
weight
underline
glow
color shift
highlight
position
opacity
only at the corresponding speech moment.
============================================================
CHARACTER SYNCHRONIZATION
============================================================
Characters must react to narration.
Examples:
Narrator says:
"the agent enters"
→ character walks/enters.
Narrator says:
"we need to isolate it"
→ character stops and isolation boundary appears.
Narrator says:
"this is dangerous"
→ concerned expression/reaction.
Narrator says:
"the request is approved"
→ positive confirmation gesture.
Do NOT continuously animate characters without narrative purpose.
============================================================
DIAGRAM SYNCHRONIZATION
============================================================
Construct diagrams according to narration.
Example:
Narrator:
"the host contains the sandbox"
→ host appears.
Narrator:
"inside the sandbox"
→ sandbox appears.
Narrator:
"the agent runs here"
→ agent node appears.
Narrator:
"the request travels through the proxy"
→ connector draws and data particle travels.
Narrator:
"the proxy checks the request"
→ proxy activates.
Narrator:
"then forwards it"
→ data continues.
Every node, connector, and data movement must correspond to the spoken
concept.
============================================================
DATA FLOW SYNCHRONIZATION
============================================================
If narration describes movement:
"request goes from A to B"
animate:
A
→ request appears
→ request starts moving
→ request travels
→ B receives request.
Do not show the completed connection before the narration describes it.
============================================================
CHART SYNCHRONIZATION
============================================================
If narration says:
"usage increases"
→ chart rises while "increases" is spoken.
If narration says:
"CPU reaches 90 percent"
→ counter counts toward 90 during the phrase.
If narration says:
"the old system is slower"
→ old bar/line becomes visibly slower or lower.
Animation must represent the spoken action.
============================================================
UI / TERMINAL SYNCHRONIZATION
============================================================
For terminal/code scenes:
Narrator:
"we run the command"
→ command types.
Narrator:
"the process starts"
→ process indicator activates.
Narrator:
"the request fails"
→ error appears.
Narrator:
"access is granted"
→ success/status changes.
Do not type the entire command instantly.
Synchronize typing speed to the narration where appropriate.
============================================================
IMAGE SYNCHRONIZATION
============================================================
If a photographic/image asset represents something being discussed:
Do not simply fade the image in at the beginning of the scene.
Reveal it when the narrator introduces the concept.
Use:
mask reveal
zoom
pan
crop
focus
highlight
overlay
to make the image participate in the explanation.
============================================================
ANIMATION START RULE
============================================================
Every animation must have:
TRIGGER PHRASE
TRIGGER TIME
ANIMATION START
ANIMATION END
PURPOSE.
Example:
{
  "triggerPhrase": "network is blocked",
  "triggerTime": 18.73,
  "animationStart": 18.73,
  "animationEnd": 19.35,
  "purpose": "show network isolation"
}
============================================================
NO PREMATURE ANIMATION
============================================================
Never:
- reveal a result before the narrator explains it
- show a conclusion before the explanation
- animate a diagram completely before narration reaches it
- show all labels simultaneously
- animate unrelated elements during important speech.
The viewer should discover the visual at approximately the same time the
narrator explains it.
============================================================
NO DELAYED ANIMATION
============================================================
Do not wait several seconds after the narrator explains something before
showing it unless the delay is intentionally used for dramatic emphasis.
Default:
speech → immediate corresponding visual action.
============================================================
PAUSE SYNCHRONIZATION
============================================================
When the narrator pauses:
DO NOT automatically introduce unrelated visuals.
Use the pause to:
- complete an animation
- hold a key visual
- emphasize a result
- allow comprehension
- prepare the next visual.
============================================================
EMPHASIS SYNCHRONIZATION
============================================================
When the narrator stresses a word or phrase:
increase visual emphasis at that exact moment.
Possible effects:
scale pulse
glow
color shift
underline
highlight
camera push
object activation
particle burst.
Example:
Narrator:
"THIS is the security boundary."
At "THIS":
→ security boundary receives emphasis.
============================================================
SENTENCE ENDING
============================================================
When the narrator finishes explaining a concept:
allow the visual to settle.
Do not immediately destroy it.
Hold the completed visual long enough for comprehension.
Then transition when the narration moves to the next concept.
============================================================
SCENE TRANSITION SYNCHRONIZATION
============================================================
Transitions should occur at:
- sentence boundaries
- conceptual boundaries
- meaningful pauses
- changes in subject.
If the narrator continues describing the same object:
DO NOT unnecessarily transition.
Instead, continue animating the existing visual.
============================================================
CONTINUOUS VISUAL STORY
============================================================
Whenever possible, let one visual become the next.
Example:
Scene 1:
sandbox appears.
Scene 2:
camera moves closer to sandbox.
Scene 3:
sandbox opens into architecture diagram.
Scene 4:
architecture diagram becomes network flow.
Avoid unrelated visual resets.
============================================================
FRAME ACCURACY
============================================================
Use the project's actual FPS.
For every event calculate:
startFrame = round(startTime * fps)
endFrame = round(endTime * fps)
Animation timing must be frame-accurate.
Never rely on arbitrary delays such as:
setTimeout
or
"wait 500ms"
when the timing can be tied directly to the Remotion timeline.
Use Remotion's timeline/frame-based animation system.
============================================================
AUDIO SYNC DATA
============================================================
Create a structured synchronization map.
Example:
{
  "scene": "scene_04",
  "events": [
    {
      "phrase": "the host",
      "start": 14.21,
      "end": 14.63,
      "visual": "host",
      "animation": "fade + scale"
    },
    {
      "phrase": "contains the sandbox",
      "start": 14.64,
      "end": 15.51,
      "visual": "sandbox boundary",
      "animation": "draw boundary"
    },
    {
      "phrase": "the agent runs inside",
      "start": 15.52,
      "end": 16.42,
      "visual": "agent",
      "animation": "enter + activate"
    }
  ]
}
============================================================
FINAL SYNCHRONIZATION CHECK
============================================================
Before rendering, verify EVERY major visual action:
[ ] Is there a corresponding spoken phrase?
[ ] Does the animation start at the phrase's timing?
[ ] Does the animation finish naturally?
[ ] Is the visual understandable while spoken?
[ ] Is anything appearing before it is explained?
[ ] Is anything appearing after the narration has moved on?
[ ] Are keyword highlights synchronized?
[ ] Are character gestures synchronized?
[ ] Are diagram nodes synchronized?
[ ] Are connectors synchronized?
[ ] Are data movements synchronized?
[ ] Are chart animations synchronized?
[ ] Are counters synchronized?
[ ] Are UI interactions synchronized?
[ ] Are image reveals synchronized?
[ ] Are transitions synchronized?
[ ] Are pauses respected?
============================================================
ABSOLUTE RULE
============================================================
DO NOT ASK:
"What animation should happen in this scene?"
ASK:
"WHAT EXACTLY IS THE NARRATOR SAYING RIGHT NOW,
AND WHAT VISUAL ACTION SHOULD HAPPEN AT THAT EXACT MOMENT
TO SHOW THE VIEWER WHAT THOSE WORDS MEAN?"
Then synchronize the animation to that speech.
THE NARRATION EXPLAINS.
THE VISUAL RESPONDS.
THE ANIMATION HAPPENS AT THE EXACT MOMENT OF MEANING.
No arbitrary animation timing.
No generic scene-wide animation.
No premature visual reveals.
No delayed visual explanations.
Every meaningful visual action must be speech-driven.
1. Use the exact timestamps from the transcription
2. Create scenes that cover the full audio duration
3. Each scene's visual elements appear at the exact frame matching the audio timestamp
UNIVERSAL HYPERFRAME / REMOTION MASTER PROMPT — 8300-LINE EDITION
Purpose: convert any narrated topic into a premium reference-style motion-design video.
VOICEOVER IS THE MASTER TIMELINE.
TRANSCRIPT IS A SEMANTIC INPUT, NOT A SUBTITLE TRACK.
DESIGN.MD IS A HARD GATE BEFORE FINAL IMPLEMENTATION.
NEVER DEFAULT TO BOTTOM-CENTER CONTENT.
NEVER LEAVE EMPTY VISUAL PAGES.
EVERY IMPORTANT VERB MUST BECOME A VISIBLE ACTION.
EVERY IMPORTANT NOUN MUST BECOME A VISUAL ENTITY WHEN PRACTICAL.
EVERY RELATIONSHIP MUST BECOME A VISIBLE RELATIONSHIP.
EVERY QUANTITY MUST BECOME A MEASURABLE VISUAL WHEN PRACTICAL.
EVERY STATE CHANGE MUST BE SHOWN AS A STATE CHANGE.
EVERY SCENE MUST CONTRIBUTE TO THE NARRATED IDEA.
THE VISUAL SHOULD PROVE THE NARRATION, NOT REPEAT IT.
THE AGENT MUST SUPPORT AUDIO-ONLY INPUT.
THE AGENT MUST SUPPORT AUDIO + TIMESTAMPED TRANSCRIPT INPUT.
THE AGENT MUST SUPPORT TRANSCRIPT-ONLY DESIGN WHEN AUDIO IS ABSENT.
IF AUDIO EXISTS, TRANSCRIBE IT BEFORE DESIGNING THE FINAL SCENES.
IF WORD TIMESTAMPS EXIST, USE THEM.
IF ONLY PHRASE/SENTENCE TIMESTAMPS EXIST, SUBDIVIDE THEM SEMANTICALLY.
IF ONLY AUDIO EXISTS, DERIVE phrase timing from transcription and audio alignment.
CREATE DESIGN.MD BEFORE IMPLEMENTING THE FINAL REMOTION VIDEO.
DESIGN.MD MUST COVER THE COMPLETE AUDIO FROM 0 TO THE END.
DESIGN.MD MUST NOT CONTAIN EMPTY PLACEHOLDER SCENES.
DESIGN.MD MUST CONTAIN A COMPLETE SEMANTIC VISUAL DICTIONARY.
DESIGN.MD MUST CONTAIN A COMPLETE ACTION-TO-ANIMATION DICTIONARY.
DESIGN.MD MUST CONTAIN SCENE LAYOUT SKETCHES.
DESIGN.MD MUST CONTAIN PHRASE-LEVEL TIMING.
DESIGN.MD MUST CONTAIN CONTINUITY AND TRANSITION RULES.
DESIGN.MD MUST CONTAIN AN IMPLEMENTATION MAP.
DESIGN.MD MUST CONTAIN A FINAL QA AUDIT.
DO NOT IMPLEMENT FINAL SCENES UNTIL DESIGN.MD PASSES THE COVERAGE AUDIT.

===== SOURCE-VIDEO DNA — NEWLY ANALYZED UPLOADED VIDEO =====
Source inspected: uploaded 1280x720, 30fps, approximately 16:10 long-form technical explainer.
Observed background: near-black charcoal, visually close to RGB 15,17,16; treat this as the base background family.
Do NOT use pure black as the default if it makes the scene feel flatter than the reference.
Keep the background visually consistent across the entire video unless a deliberate full-scene state change is required.
Do NOT change background hue from scene to scene merely to make scenes different.
Observed primary visual language: thin outlined technical sketches, simple geometric objects, small UI-like labels, measurement bars, nodes, containers, chips, devices, and diagrams.
Observed dominant accent family: warm signal yellow for price/value/active capacity/highlight states.
Observed warning family: red/coral for rejection, cost emphasis, failure, danger, crossed-out states, and constraint boundaries.
Observed informational family: restrained electric/cyan blue for neutral technical emphasis, selected controls, and informational states.
Observed neutral family: off-white for primary objects and primary numerical values; muted gray for secondary labels, axes, inactive objects, and metadata.
Keep accent colors sparse. The reference does NOT paint every object bright.
Use color semantically: yellow = active/value/capacity; red = warning/cost/rejection; blue = informational/selected; white = structure/primary information; gray = secondary/inactive.
Never introduce random green, purple, orange, pink, gradient rainbow palettes, or glossy SaaS colors unless the source material absolutely requires them.
Prefer flat fills, flat strokes, and restrained contrast over gradients.
Do not use heavy glow as a substitute for design.
Do not use glassmorphism.
Do not use 3D chrome.
Do not use photorealistic objects when a clean technical sketch communicates the concept better.
Observed stroke language: thin clean outlines with rounded or slightly softened geometry.
Use consistent stroke weights across an object family.
Use a slightly heavier stroke only for active/emphasized elements.
Do not create thick cartoon outlines.
Do not create hand-drawn wobble unless the source concept genuinely benefits from a sketch-like irregularity.
Observed composition: substantial negative space surrounds a compact visual system.
Negative space is intentional, not an empty page.
Do not fill every corner with decorative particles.
Do not interpret negative space as a reason to enlarge everything to full-screen.
Default composition should often live in the lower-middle information field, echoing the uploaded video.
Lower-middle does NOT mean a permanent subtitle shelf.
The main diagram, object, chart, or system should occupy the lower-middle field while labels attach directly to it.
Allow important numbers or hero objects to rise toward the center when they become the semantic focus.
Use the upper half for large quantitative callouts, contextual labels, or empty breathing room when the reference grammar calls for it.
Do not place every sentence as a separate bottom-center card.
Observed visual density: sparse individual objects, but high semantic density.
Prefer 3-8 meaningful objects over dozens of decorative objects.
Every object must have a job: entity, state, relation, measurement, evidence, or transition carrier.
Observed text density: text is present but secondary to geometry and objects.
Use labels, prices, units, axis values, tiny state tags, and short annotations.
Do NOT write full explanatory paragraphs on screen.
Do NOT convert narration into subtitles.
Do NOT use a headline for every spoken sentence.
Use a short label only when the visual object would otherwise be ambiguous.
Use numbers when numbers are actually part of the narration.
Use units next to measurements rather than repeating prose.
Use labels attached to the object, not detached caption blocks.
Observed hero-number treatment: large off-white numbers can become the focal point when the narration discusses a specific amount.
Hero numbers may sit above a measurement or comparison structure.
Secondary unit text should be smaller and muted.
Observed comparison treatment: long horizontal measurement lines with a moving dot/marker and compact axis labels.
Observed cost treatment: red horizontal reference line, red endpoint/marker, and yellow value/indicator when the narration emphasizes price or a threshold.
Observed capacity treatment: repeated yellow rectangular cells inside a thin container, visually resembling memory/chip cells.
Use repeated cells for capacity, tokens, memory, throughput, or repeated units when appropriate.
Observed device treatment: simplified outlined hardware silhouettes, not photorealistic product renders.
Observed person treatment: minimal line/icon human figure, not a realistic portrait, when the concept is a person/user.
Observed computer/device treatment: simple monitor/laptop/device outline with a small internal screen or symbol.
Observed chip treatment: rectangular chip with repeated pins/cells or modular blocks.
Observed server/rack treatment: simple rectangular chassis/rack geometry with internal slots or repeated units.
Observed data treatment: compact pills, nodes, packets, lines, and repeated blocks.
Observed architecture treatment: containers connected by thin lines, with active paths highlighted.
Observed state treatment: outline remains stable while accent color or a small internal mark changes.
Observed failure treatment: red X, red barrier, red lock, red rejection mark, or red emphasized boundary.
Observed transition treatment: objects often disappear, collapse, transform, or clear into the next small visual rather than using a full-screen fade.
Use geometric morphs whenever two concepts share a visual structure.
Use a line as a transition carrier when one concept leads into another.
Use a horizontal bar as a transition carrier when moving between quantitative scenes.
Use a repeated cell grid as a transition carrier when moving between memory/model/hardware concepts.
Use a node or packet as a transition carrier when moving between systems.
Use a device outline as a transition carrier when moving between hardware comparisons.
Observed drawing behavior: elements frequently appear by progressive line/shape construction.
Prefer stroke drawing, path reveal, scale-from-small, clipping, masking, cell-by-cell activation, and marker travel.
Use small staggered reveals for repeated cells.
Use synchronized drawing for related connector lines.
Use short, decisive movement rather than slow cinematic drift.
Animation should feel engineered, precise, and timed to speech.
Do not animate everything continuously.
Allow objects to settle after their explanatory action.
Use micro-motion only when it supports active state or continuity.
Observed visual rhythm: build → emphasize → hold → transform/clear → build next concept.
Use this rhythm as the default scene micro-structure.
Do not make every scene a build → fade → build loop.
Use transformation and continuity when the next scene is causally related.
Observed emphasis rhythm: a number/object may arrive, then a marker/line/indicator activates after it.
Therefore, separate entity arrival from semantic emphasis when narration has that sequence.
Observed quantitative rhythm: reveal the measurement structure first, then reveal the value/marker, then emphasize the relevant endpoint.
Do not reveal the answer before the narrator reaches the answer.
Observed system rhythm: show the container or architecture, then populate it, then show the active state, then show the consequence.
Use the same sequence for software, hardware, AI, finance, networks, or any technical topic when semantically appropriate.
Observed transitions often preserve the same spatial scale rather than hard-resetting the entire composition.
Use camera framing and object transformation to preserve continuity.
Do not use excessive camera zooms.
Camera movement should be subtle and purposeful.
Prefer 2D motion-graphics camera language over fake 3D.
Do not turn every diagram into a rotating 3D scene.
===== END SOURCE-VIDEO DNA =====
===== VISUAL-COMPILER PRINCIPLE =====
Input is not text to decorate.
Input is meaning to visualize.
For every transcript segment perform: transcript → semantic proposition → entities → relationships → states → actions → visual sketch → composition → animation → exact frame timing.
Before writing any on-screen text, ask: can geometry, movement, iconography, measurement, or transformation communicate this idea instead?
If yes, use the visual and reduce text to a label or measurement.
If no, use the smallest amount of text needed.
The narration explains the idea; the visual demonstrates the idea.
Do not make the audience read what the narrator is already saying.
Make the audience see what the narrator is saying.
===== SKETCH-FIRST COMPILER =====
For every important noun, create a visual sketch before considering a text label.
Server → outlined rack/chassis with slots, ports, status lights, or stacked compute units.
Database → cylindrical or stacked storage symbol with records flowing in/out.
API → two systems connected by a request/response line with directional packets.
Request → small packet leaving a source and traveling along a connector.
Response → packet returning on a distinct return path.
Model → compute block or model container with internal layered/token structure.
LLM → model container with token stream entering and generated token stream leaving.
Token → repeated small tile/pill/character block.
Context window → bounded horizontal token container whose capacity fills.
KV cache → persistent memory bank of repeated cells attached to the active inference path.
RAM → memory grid whose cells fill as allocation increases.
VRAM → dedicated memory block visually attached to GPU/accelerator.
GPU → outlined accelerator board/chip with repeated compute cells.
CPU → outlined compute unit with multiple processing lanes.
Quantization → dense high-resolution cells transform into fewer/coarser cells with a visible representation change.
Compression → representation physically contracts while preserving the conceptual payload.
RAG → document sheets → chunk blocks → embedding/vector field → retrieval path → context box → model.
Embedding → points/vectors distributed in a spatial field with related items clustering.
Vector database → searchable field/grid containing vector points plus retrieval path.
Agent → central controller/model connected to tools, memory, environment, and output.
Tool call → agent sends a packet into a tool node and receives a result packet.
Memory → persistent storage block that survives between actions.
Latency → packet path with visible time markers or delayed arrival.
Throughput → repeated packets/cells moving through a channel per unit time.
Bandwidth → wide/narrow channel whose capacity is visibly constrained.
Bottleneck → pipeline section narrows and packet spacing increases.
Queue → repeated packets waiting in a clearly ordered lane.
Cache hit → request reaches a nearby cache and returns quickly.
Cache miss → request passes through cache to deeper storage.
Load balancing → requests distribute across multiple server nodes.
Scaling → one server visually becomes several parallel server nodes.
Deployment → build artifact moves from development container into a runtime/server container.
CI/CD → code → test → build → deploy pipeline with stage activation.
Git branch → one code path splits into branches and later converges.
Merge → two paths physically converge into one.
Bug → error marker attached to the exact component causing the issue.
Debugging → camera/inspection focuses on the faulty component and traces the causal path.
Security → boundary/gate surrounding protected resources.
Authentication → identity enters a gate and receives an authenticated state.
Authorization → authenticated identity reaches permission gate and either passes or is blocked.
Privacy → data remains inside a visible boundary rather than traveling outward.
Cloud → remote infrastructure boundary outside the local-device boundary.
Local AI → model and compute visibly contained inside the user's local machine boundary.
Hybrid AI → local and remote boundaries connected by controlled traffic.
Cost → cumulative value grows along a measurement structure rather than appearing as unexplained text.
Break-even → two measured curves/paths approach and cross at the narrated point.
Benchmark → repeated test inputs produce aligned measured outputs.
Performance → speed/throughput/capacity shown through a measurable visual system.
Error rate → repeated trials with a fraction of failures highlighted.
Reliability → repeated successful cycles with occasional failures shown proportionally when supported by data.
Comparison → two matched visual structures sharing the same scale or coordinate system.
Alternative → two paths or devices shown in parallel with consistent geometry.
Recommendation → only after evidence is established; visually distinguish observed facts from editorial conclusion.
===== ACTION-WORD VISUALIZATION =====
Do not display the word 'rejected' as the main visual for rejection.
Instead physically reject the object: stop it at a gate, stamp it, cross it, bounce it back, or redirect it.
Do not display 'blocked' as a large title.
Instead create a visible barrier and show the packet stopping.
Do not display 'faster' as a large word.
Instead shorten the travel path, accelerate the packet, reduce the measured time, or show a faster progress marker.
Do not display 'slower' as a large word.
Instead visibly delay the packet, lengthen the path, or reduce the rate.
Do not display 'more' as a large word.
Instead add objects, increase cells, raise a bar, or expand a count.
Do not display 'less' as a large word.
Instead remove objects, shrink a bar, reduce cells, or contract the representation.
Do not display 'expensive' as the explanation.
Instead build the cost visually with a large value, reference line, and emphasized endpoint.
Do not display 'cheap' as the explanation.
Instead show the lower measured cost relative to the same scale.
Do not display 'powerful' as the visual.
Instead show greater capacity, more compute cells, larger throughput, or the documented metric.
Do not display 'limited' as the visual.
Instead show a filled boundary, constrained capacity, or blocked expansion.
Do not display 'connects' as text.
Instead draw the connector between the entities.
Do not display 'disconnects' as text.
Instead remove/break the connector and show the state change.
Do not display 'splits' as text.
Instead physically divide the object into multiple objects.
Do not display 'merges' as text.
Instead physically converge the objects.
Do not display 'builds' as text.
Instead progressively construct the object from lines/shapes.
Do not display 'grows' as text.
Instead scale or extend the measured structure.
Do not display 'shrinks' as text.
Instead contract it visibly.
Do not display 'moves' as text.
Instead move the object.
Do not display 'flows' as text.
Instead animate packets along a path.
Do not display 'waits' as text.
Instead queue the objects and delay their motion.
Do not display 'retrieves' as text.
Instead show data leaving storage and arriving at the active context.
Do not display 'stores' as text.
Instead show the object entering and remaining in a storage container.
Do not display 'forgets' as text.
Instead visibly remove the object from persistent memory.
Do not display 'copies' as text.
Instead duplicate the object and preserve identity cues.
Do not display 'updates' as text.
Instead replace/transform the old state into the new state.
Do not display 'fails' as text.
Instead interrupt the process at the failure location and use the reference red failure grammar.
Do not display 'recovers' as text.
Instead reverse the failure state and resume the process.
Do not display 'optimizes' as text.
Instead transform the inefficient path into a more efficient measured path.
Do not display 'compresses' as text.
Instead physically pack the representation into a smaller form.
Do not display 'quantizes' as text.
Instead visibly reduce representation granularity.
Do not display 'scales' as text.
Instead duplicate/parallelize compute nodes.
Do not display 'deploys' as text.
Instead move the artifact into a runtime container and activate it.
===== TEXT MINIMIZATION =====
Text is an annotation layer, never the default visual substrate.
Allowed text: short labels, numbers, units, state tags, tiny metadata, axis values, concise callouts.
Preferred text density: sparse.
Do not place a paragraph in the visual field unless the source itself is a document/screenshot being shown as evidence.
Do not use three or four explanatory sentences on screen while the narrator speaks the same sentences.
Do not make every scene title-heavy.
Do not create title cards merely because a new topic starts.
Let the object, diagram, or transformation communicate the topic change.
Use typography as a visual object only when the narration is specifically about a word, number, quote, code token, or textual artifact.
===== COLOR CONSISTENCY =====
Define one global palette at project initialization and reuse it across all scenes.
Background base: near-black charcoal family centered around #0F1110.
Background must remain stable across scenes.
Primary off-white: approximately #F0F2EF.
Secondary neutral: approximately #737773.
Structure outline: approximately #4A4D49.
Yellow accent: approximately #F4D94A.
Red accent: approximately #D92F45.
Blue accent: approximately #2B9BD7.
Use these as a restrained system, not as mandatory simultaneous colors.
Most scenes should use neutral structure + one dominant accent.
Two accents may coexist when the narration compares two states, but do not turn the scene into a rainbow.
Red should mean something.
Yellow should mean something.
Blue should mean something.
White should establish the main structure.
Gray should subordinate.
Do not recolor the same object arbitrarily between scenes.
Do not use color changes as decoration.
===== SIZE CONSISTENCY =====
Use a consistent visual scale system across the whole video.
Primary hero object/number should have a clearly dominant scale.
Secondary objects should be smaller but still readable at 1280x720 and 1920x1080.
Micro-labels must remain legible and should not become tiny unreadable noise.
Do not randomly make one server icon enormous and another microscopic unless scale has semantic meaning.
Use relative scale intentionally for quantity, hierarchy, distance, or capacity.
Keep repeated object families the same size.
Keep repeated cell grids consistent in cell dimensions.
Keep connector thickness consistent.
Keep label sizing consistent by semantic level.
===== COMPOSITION GRAMMAR =====
Default reference composition: compact visual system in the lower-middle/central-lower field with generous negative space.
Use lower-middle for the main technical diagram when there is no reason to occupy the full frame.
Move the visual upward when a large numerical hero or vertical architecture requires it.
Move the visual sideways when comparing two alternatives.
Use left/right split for A/B comparisons.
Use center for a transformation happening inside a container.
Use a horizontal axis for price, speed, capacity, or time comparisons.
Use a vertical stack for hierarchy or sequential layers.
Use a wide horizontal pipeline for network/process explanations.
Use a bounded rectangle for a system, device, or environment.
Use nested boundaries for local/cloud/security/privacy concepts.
Use the bottom edge only when it is semantically useful; never use it as a caption shelf.
Keep the main visual optically balanced, not mathematically centered by default.
===== TRANSITION GRAMMAR =====
Prefer object-to-object transformation.
Prefer line-to-line transformation.
Prefer marker-to-marker continuity.
Prefer grid-to-grid continuity.
Prefer container-to-container continuity.
Prefer packet-to-packet continuity.
Prefer camera reframing over hard reset when the concept is related.
Use clear/erase only when the narration explicitly changes subject.
Use a brief fade only as a secondary technique, never the dominant transition style.
Do not use cinematic whip pans unless the source style and narration justify them.
Do not use random zoom transitions.
Do not use spinning transitions.
Do not use generic presentation-slide transitions.
===== DESIGN.MD VISUAL-FIRST GATE =====
Before implementation, DESIGN.MD must include a 'VISUAL COMPILER TABLE' for every meaningful transcript phrase.
Each row must contain: phrase, meaning, noun entities, action verbs, relationship, state, visual sketch, spatial placement, colors, size hierarchy, animation, exact timing, and transition carrier.
For every noun row, the visual sketch must be described as an object, diagram, UI, icon, chart, physical metaphor, or system structure.
For every action row, the visual must physically perform the action.
For every comparison row, both sides must share a consistent measurement frame.
For every number row, the visual must make the number meaningful.
For every abstract concept, the agent must attempt at least three visual metaphors before selecting one.
Choose the metaphor that communicates the mechanism with the least text.
Do not select a metaphor merely because it is easy to code.
===== AUDIO-ONLY WORKFLOW =====
If only audio is supplied, extract the audio duration and transcribe it.
Create phrase-level or word-level timestamps from the transcription.
Segment the narration by semantic shifts, not only pauses.
Generate the complete transcript-to-visual compiler table.
Create DESIGN.MD.
Run the visual coverage audit.
Only then implement Remotion.
If audio and transcript timestamps are supplied, trust supplied timestamps when they are coherent and use audio as the timing authority.
If transcript has no timestamps, align it to the audio before scene design.
If audio contains pauses, do not automatically make blank visual pages; maintain a purposeful visual hold or a controlled transition.
If a pause is dramatic, hold the previous visual in a stable state rather than introducing random decoration.
===== ANY-TOPIC UNIVERSALITY =====
The system must work for software, AI, hardware, science, finance, business, history, product explanations, tutorials, workflows, comparisons, reviews, and abstract concepts.
Do not force every topic into a server diagram.
Choose visual grammar from the meaning of the topic.
For biology, use anatomical/system sketches when appropriate.
For physics, use measured diagrams, vectors, fields, particles, and transformations.
For finance, use price lines, flows, ledgers, accumulation, and comparison structures.
For product explanations, use object sketches, component callouts, measurements, and state changes.
For history, use timelines, maps, objects, documents, and spatial relationships.
For business workflows, use people/system nodes, process lanes, documents, decisions, and metrics.
For coding, use code fragments only when necessary, connected to actual system behavior.
For AI, prefer architecture, token, memory, compute, retrieval, and data-flow visuals.
For hardware, prefer component sketches, buses, memory cells, ports, boards, and measurement structures.
For abstract ideas, construct a concrete visual metaphor and keep it consistent.
===== FINAL STYLE LOCK =====
The final video must feel like one coherent visual system, not a collection of unrelated scenes.
Background remains consistent.
Palette remains consistent.
Stroke language remains consistent.
Object scale remains consistent.
Text density remains restrained.
Visual explanation dominates textual explanation.
Animation is synchronized to speech.
Transitions are motivated.
Negative space is intentional.
Lower-middle composition is the default reference posture, not an absolute rule.
Every major transcript concept becomes something the viewer can see.
Every major transcript action becomes something the viewer can watch happen.
Every major number becomes a measurable visual.
Every major comparison becomes a matched visual comparison.
Every major state change becomes a visible state change.
Every scene must look designed, not auto-generated.
